```{r}
devtools::clean_dll()
devtools::load_all()
library(geepack)
```

# Purpose

The overall intervention test in `test_processor()` compares the treatment and
control outcome means with an ordinary two-sample statistic that treats every
participant as independent. BetterBirth (like every study we work with) is
**clustered**: participants are nested in facilities (`site_name`), and outcomes
within a facility are correlated. Ignoring that correlation makes the naive test
overstate precision (p-value biased downward).

This file demonstrates, for the BB binary example already shipped with the
package, how the overall test changes once facility clustering is accounted for.
It reports the intra-cluster correlation (ICC) three ways, and compares the naive
test with two textbook-faithful clustered tests.

The ICC estimator follows the ANOVA method in Donner & Klar, *Design and Analysis
of Cluster Randomization Trials in Health Research*, pp. 84-85, applied to the
(0,1) binary outcome. Nothing here changes the package; the adjustments are
computed inline so the versions sit side by side.

A design caveat that governs everything below: BetterBirth is **not** a clean
cluster-randomized trial. Treatment status varies pre/post *within* a facility,
and 25 of 36 facilities appear in only one arm, so arm and facility are partly
confounded. That is why (a) a single ICC number is ambiguous, and (b) the choice
of clustered test matters. Both points are made explicit below.

# 1. The package's current (no-ICC) overall test

`lago_optimization()` runs the overall test through `test_processor()` and prints
it, but does not return it in the result object, so we call `test_processor()`
directly here to capture the exact statistic the package computes. This is the
current no-clustering two-sample test.

```{r}
bb_data <- LAGO::BB_data
bb_data$group <- ifelse(bb_data$pre_post == 0, "control", "treatment")

# the overall test exactly as the package computes it (no clustering term)
naive <- test_processor(
  data = bb_data,
  outcome_type = "binary",
  outcome_name = "pp3_oxytocin_mother"
)
cat(sprintf("NAIVE (no ICC):  t = %.2f   p = %.3g\n",
            naive$test_stat, naive$p_val))
```

# 2. Estimate the ICC (Donner & Klar, pp. 84-85)

The ICC estimator is a one-way random-effects ANOVA on the (0,1) outcome:

$$\hat\rho = \frac{\text{MSC} - \text{MSW}}{\text{MSC} + (m_0 - 1)\,\text{MSW}}$$

where MSC / MSW are the between- and within-cluster mean squares and
$m_0 = \left(M - \sum_i m_i^2 / M\right) / (K - 1)$ is the adjusted mean cluster
size. Negative estimates are set to 0. This is the one-way (single-group)
specialization of the Donner & Klar p.85 formula, which in its general two-group
form uses deviations about the *group* rate and a $(K - 2)$ denominator; with
$K = 36$ facilities the difference is immaterial ($\Delta\hat\rho \approx
0.0001$). We report a *response-scale* (probability-scale) ICC, matching the
textbook's definition on the (0,1) observations -- it is not a logistic
latent-scale ICC and the two are not directly comparable.

```{r}
# Donner-Klar one-way ANOVA ICC on a response vector.
dk_icc <- function(response, cluster) {
  ok <- !is.na(response) & !is.na(cluster)
  y <- response[ok]
  cl <- factor(cluster[ok])
  N <- length(y)
  K <- nlevels(cl)
  ni <- as.numeric(table(cl))
  grand_mean <- mean(y)
  cluster_means <- tapply(y, cl, mean)
  MSC <- sum(ni * (cluster_means - grand_mean)^2) / (K - 1)
  MSW <- sum(tapply(y, cl, function(v) sum((v - mean(v))^2))) / (N - K)
  m0 <- (N - sum(ni^2) / N) / (K - 1)
  rho <- (MSC - MSW) / (MSC + (m0 - 1) * MSW)
  rho <- max(rho, 0)
  list(rho = rho, m0 = m0, K = K, N = N,
       design_effect = 1 + (m0 - 1) * rho)
}
```

Because arm and facility are confounded here, no single ICC is "the" ICC. We
report all of the sensible quantities and label them explicitly.

```{r}
# (a) RAW pooled, both arms, arm ignored. This folds the treatment jump
#     (control ~0.30 -> treatment ~0.87) into the between-cluster mean square,
#     so it is INFLATED by the intervention effect and is NOT a true facility
#     ICC. Reported only to be transparent about what "no adjustment at all"
#     gives.
icc_raw <- dk_icc(bb_data$pp3_oxytocin_mother, bb_data$site_name)

# (b) WITHIN-ARM ICCs, computed in each arm separately (design-honest "raw"
#     clustering -- never mixes the arm shift into any variance term).
ctrl <- bb_data[bb_data$group == "control", ]
trt  <- bb_data[bb_data$group == "treatment", ]
icc_ctrl <- dk_icc(ctrl$pp3_oxytocin_mother, ctrl$site_name)
icc_trt  <- dk_icc(trt$pp3_oxytocin_mother,  trt$site_name)

# (c) ARM-ADJUSTED residual ICC: pool both arms but first remove the arm mean
#     via a GLM, then compute the ICC on the residuals. This is the
#     "within-facility correlation after accounting for arm". na.exclude keeps
#     the residual vector full length so it stays aligned to site_name even if
#     a covariate has NAs.
resid_arm <- residuals(
  glm(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ group, data = bb_data,
      family = binomial, na.action = na.exclude),
  type = "response"
)
icc_before <- dk_icc(resid_arm, bb_data$site_name)

# ... and ALSO removing facility volume (a cluster-level covariate).
resid_vol <- residuals(
  glm(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ group + birth_volume_100, data = bb_data,
      family = binomial, na.action = na.exclude),
  type = "response"
)
icc_after <- dk_icc(resid_vol, bb_data$site_name)

cat(sprintf("Facilities (clusters) K = %d,  adjusted mean size m0 = %.1f\n\n",
            icc_before$K, icc_before$m0))
cat("ICC of BB oxytocin within facility (response scale):\n")
cat(sprintf("  (a) raw pooled, arm ignored .............. %.3f  [ARTIFACT: inflated by the treatment effect]\n",
            icc_raw$rho))
cat(sprintf("  (b) within control arm .................. %.3f\n", icc_ctrl$rho))
cat(sprintf("      within treatment arm ................ %.3f\n", icc_trt$rho))
cat(sprintf("  (c) arm-adjusted residual (before volume) %.3f  (DE = %.1f)\n",
            icc_before$rho, icc_before$design_effect))
cat(sprintf("      arm-adjusted residual (after volume)  %.3f  (DE = %.1f)\n",
            icc_after$rho, icc_after$design_effect))
```

Reading these: the raw 0.55 is an artifact of the pre/post design and should not
be quoted as the ICC. The design-honest facility clustering is substantial and
**not constant across arms** (~0.48 control vs ~0.31 treatment), so the single
exchangeable-ICC assumption is itself an approximation. The arm-adjusted residual
ICC is ~0.34, dropping to ~0.27 once facility volume is also removed -- i.e.
facility volume explains part, but not most, of the between-facility variation.

# 3. The overall test, done cluster-honestly

The naive test in Section 1 assumes 6124 independent observations. Two
textbook-faithful ways to respect the facility clustering:

**(i) Cluster-level t-test (Donner & Klar p.87).** Reduce each facility-arm to
its event rate and run a two-sample t on those rates, with $K - 2$ degrees of
freedom. This is the "collapse to cluster summaries" test. Caveat for BB: the 11
dual-arm facilities contribute two (non-independent) cells, which this test
treats as independent, and every facility is weighted equally regardless of size.

```{r}
cell_rates <- aggregate(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ site_name + group,
                        data = bb_data, FUN = mean)
cl_t <- t.test(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ group, data = cell_rates, var.equal = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("(i)  cluster-level t-test:  t = %.2f  df = %.0f  p = %.3g\n",
            cl_t$statistic, cl_t$parameter, cl_t$p.value))
```

**(ii) GEE with exchangeable working correlation, cluster = facility, robust
(sandwich) SE.** This is the design-based inference: it models the
within-facility correlation and produces a cluster-robust test for the treatment
effect. We show it both unadjusted and adjusted for facility volume.

```{r}
d_gee <- bb_data[order(bb_data$site_name), ]
d_gee$site <- factor(d_gee$site_name)

gee_unadj <- geeglm(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ group, id = site,
                    data = d_gee, family = binomial, corstr = "exchangeable")
gee_adj   <- geeglm(pp3_oxytocin_mother ~ group + birth_volume_100, id = site,
                    data = d_gee, family = binomial, corstr = "exchangeable")

gee_row <- function(fit, label) {
  s <- summary(fit)$coefficients["grouptreatment", ]
  z <- s[["Estimate"]] / s[["Std.err"]]
  cat(sprintf("(ii) GEE %-22s beta = %.3f  robust SE = %.3f  z = %.2f  p = %.4f\n",
              label, s[["Estimate"]], s[["Std.err"]], z, s[["Pr(>|W|)"]]))
}
gee_row(gee_unadj, "(volume unadjusted):")
gee_row(gee_adj,   "(volume adjusted):  ")
```

# Takeaway

```{r}
cat(sprintf("NAIVE (no clustering):            p = %.3g   (t = %.1f, treats 6124 obs as independent)\n",
            naive$p_val, naive$test_stat))
cat(sprintf("Cluster-level t (D&K p.87):       p = %.3g\n", cl_t$p.value))
sg_un <- summary(gee_unadj)$coefficients["grouptreatment", ]
sg_ad <- summary(gee_adj)$coefficients["grouptreatment", ]
cat(sprintf("GEE exchangeable, volume-unadj:   p = %.4f\n", sg_un[["Pr(>|W|)"]]))
cat(sprintf("GEE exchangeable, volume-adj:     p = %.4f\n", sg_ad[["Pr(>|W|)"]]))
```

The clustering is severe: facility ICC ~0.3-0.5, design effect ~50, so the naive
test overstates the effective sample size by roughly a factor of 50.

The result this drives home -- and the reason clustering is not a formality here
-- is that the different clustered tests **disagree**, and one of them makes the
effect only marginal:

1. **The naive test (p ~ 0) is not trustworthy.** It ignores that oxytocin
   administration is largely a facility-level practice (site rates 0% to ~99%).

2. **GEE unadjusted for facility volume is only marginal (p ~ 0.07).** With 25 of
   36 facilities in a single arm, treatment is nearly confounded with facility;
   once the within-facility correlation is honored, the raw treatment contrast is
   not clearly significant.

3. **Adjusting for facility volume restores significance (GEE p < 0.001).**
   Facility volume acts as a suppressor here: conditioning on it sharpens the
   treatment contrast (beta ~1.2 -> ~2.8). This is a concrete example of Donna's
   point -- the clustered analysis and the facility-volume adjustment together
   change the conclusion, whereas the naive test hides it.

4. **The cluster-level t (p ~ 2e-11) looks decisive but is optimistic for BB:**
   it treats the 47 facility-arm cells as independent (double-counting the 11
   dual-arm facilities) and ignores facility volume. It is the right test for a
   clean cluster-randomized design, not for this partly-confounded pre/post one.

Bottom line for the package: the overall test should offer a cluster-aware option
(GEE / sandwich SE is already used on the confidence-set path), and analyses on
clustered data should report the ICC and adjust for cluster-level covariates.
Even Donner & Klar's own example (rho = 0.01, cluster size 100) inflates the
naive chi-square ~2x; at BB's ICC the naive test is off by far more, and here it
is the difference between "obviously significant" and "depends on the adjustment."
